The White grouper, Epinephelus aeneus, is a commercially important serranid found throughout the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, where it supports significant artisanal fisheries. Recent growth studies based on otolith readings from the Gulf of Gabès suggest that the species exhibits indeterminate growth, with the largest individuals recorded reaching a formidable ultimate total length of 120 cm [Li = 120 cm]. This notable body size is accompanied by a correspondingly high maximum wet weight, with the heaviest adults attaining an ultimate wet weight of 24600 grams [Wwi = 24600 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions for the species. The allometric relationship underpinning this mass is consistent with the robust, deep-bodied morphology characteristic of large groupers, which are apex predators in rocky reef habitats. Such substantial dimensions imply a significant metabolic investment in somatic growth over the species' life cycle, particularly during the protracted juvenile phase that precedes the onset of reproductive activity. Field surveys indicate that individuals of this size are relatively rare, suggesting that fishing pressure selectively removes the oldest and largest members of the population, thereby truncating the size structure and potentially impacting reproductive output due to the loss of highly fecund, dominant spawners.

Sexual maturation in Epinephelus aeneus follows a pattern common to many protogynous serranids, with puberty occurring at a relatively modest body size compared to the species' asymptotic length. Based on histological examination of gonadal tissue from individuals collected in Senegalese waters, the total length at puberty has been estimated at 55 cm [Lp = 55 cm], a threshold that corresponds to approximately 46% of the maximum recorded length for the species. This size at first maturity appears to be relatively invariant across different populations, although local environmental conditions and fishing intensity may influence the age at which this length is attained. The onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males is tightly coupled to this size benchmark, after which individuals transition from a primarily somatic growth trajectory to one that includes regular reproductive investment. The identification of this length threshold is critical for fisheries management, as it allows the establishment of minimum landing sizes designed to ensure that a majority of individuals have had the opportunity to spawn at least once before entering the fishery.

Reproductive output in the White grouper is strongly influenced by female body size and local thermal conditions, with the maximum reproduction rate being observed at a stable water temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C]. Under these conditions, a fully mature female produces approximately 38000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 38000 eggs per spawning event], and can achieve approximately 100 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 100 spawning events per year], yielding an average daily output of approximately 10410 eggs per day. This figure represents an exceptionally high fecundity for a temperate grouper species, reflecting the batch-spawning strategy that characterizes the genus Epinephelus, wherein multiple clutches are released over a protracted spawning period lasting several months. The estimated values were derived from a combination of batch fecundity counts and spawning frequency determinations made from ovarian histology. The seasonal timing of these events is closely tied to the 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C] isotherm, which appears to function as a thermal trigger for gamete maturation and final oocyte hydration prior to release.

The early life history of Epinephelus aeneus is characterized by a pelagic larval phase that begins with the emergence of a small, yolk-dependent larva following the completion of embryonic development within the transparent, pelagic egg. The wet weight at birth for a newly hatched larva is estimated at 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a value derived from the mean egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters, which yields an egg volume of approximately 0.27 microliters assuming a spherical geometry. This remarkably small initial mass places the species among the more fecund marine teleosts, which compensate for high larval mortality with an immense numerical output of minute offspring. The lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-hatching, a period during which the mouth remains closed and the digestive tract is still undergoing differentiation. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs when the yolk-sac is nearly fully resorbed and the larva attains a mouth gape sufficient to capture its first prey, typically rotifers or small copepod nauplii, marking a critical bottleneck for survival in the planktonic environment.

Longevity under natural conditions for the White grouper has been assessed through bomb radiocarbon dating of otolith cores from individuals captured in the Mediterranean, with the oldest confirmed specimen reaching a maximum lifespan of 8030 days [am = 8030 days] at a temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C]. This remarkable longevity, equivalent to approximately 22 years, positions Epinephelus aeneus as one of the longer-lived members of the Serranidae, a trait that is closely linked to its relatively slow growth rate and delayed reproductive maturation. The lifespan estimate was derived from individuals maintained at a water temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], which represents the mean annual thermal regime experienced by the species across much of its distributional range. This relatively cool thermal environment is thought to slow the rate of physiological aging, as metabolic rate scales positively with temperature in ectotherms, thereby extending the potential for somatic maintenance and repair processes. Such extended longevity carries significant implications for population resilience, as it allows a multi-decadal reproductive window that can buffer the population against sporadic recruitment failures, a demographic strategy common among long-lived, iteroparous marine fishes.
